answers.verdict: The reviewer is right on every point. busy_cycles contains the join wait, the join itself and the AVX-512 scoring of the pages that a pass writes, predict.py divides all of it by a kernel factor, and the page's attention wait (wall of worker 0 minus mean busy time) mixes the wait for Q, the wait for K and V and a worker offset, so it cannot give the K and V wait alone. A measured A/B on delphi-3bda confirms the consequence: with the 128-wide kernel on, the whole busy time of a prefill pass fell 1.88 times at prompt 1,024, where the kernel factor is 2.95 to 3.05. With the prefill factor applied only to the part of the busy time that grows with the K tokens in full pages, Part B reads 4 to 22 % (range 2 to 26 %) instead of 5 to 24 % (4 to 28 %), Parts A and B read 32 to 41 % (20 to 47 %) instead of 34 to 42 % (22 to 48 %), and decode does not change because its factor is already a ratio of whole busy times.

changes.place: Words used here, entry 'attention busy time, attention wait'
changes.old_text: attention busy time, attention wait: busy time is the time an attention worker spends on attention jobs without its waits for input. The wait is the rest of the job's wall time.
changes.new_text:
attention busy time: the time of the attention jobs on one attention worker, without the worker's waits for the queries (Q) and for K and V. It contains four parts: the scoring of the full pages of earlier passes, the scoring of the pages that the pass in progress writes, the join, and the join wait. The page gives the mean over the 40 workers.
join, join wait: the join is the last step of an attention job. It adds the partial results of the workers into one result per token. The join wait is the time that a worker waits in the join until the other workers have finished their scoring. It is part of the busy time.
full-page time: the part of the attention busy time of a prefill pass that is spent on the full pages of earlier passes (est.). Part B makes only this part faster.
attention wait: the wall time of the attention jobs on attention worker 0, minus the mean busy time. It contains the worker's wait for Q at the start of a job and its wait for K and V in the middle of a job. tron has no timer for one of these waits alone.

changes.new_text:
Prefill: the factor divides the full-page time only. The AMX kernel replaces the scoring of the full pages of earlier passes. The pages that the pass in progress writes stay on the AVX-512 path [Ref8]. They contain 12.6 % of the scored K tokens of a pass at prompt 1,024, 3.1 % at prompt 4,096 and 1.6 % at prompt 8,192 [Ref9]. The join and the join wait are not kernel work.
Size of the full-page time. The busy time without the join wait fits a straight line: a fixed part per pass, plus 67 ns of CPU time per K token in full pages. The error of the line is below 0.1 ms at each of the three prompt lengths [Ref18]. The full-page time is the part that grows with the K tokens (est.). It is 51 % of the busy time with 1 user at prompt 1,024, 72 % with 8 users at prompt 1,024, and 88 to 96 % at prompt 8,192. The other part does not change in the model. It is 3.0 to 3.8 ms per pass with 1 user and 9.6 to 10.4 ms with 8 users, join wait included.
The join wait of a prefill pass does not grow with the kernel work. From prompt 1,024 to prompt 8,192 the K tokens in full pages grow 9 times. The join wait grows 1.1 to 1.6 times.
Check against a measurement. On delphi-3bda the same statistics were recorded for qwen-3-4b with the 128-wide kernel on and off (8 users, prompt 1,024, one run per arm) [Ref23]. The kernel scored every K token of the full pages. It scored no K token of the pages that the pass wrote. The busy time per pass fell 1.88 times. The join wait rose from 4.1 to 12.0 ms. The pass wall fell by 99.7 ms, and the busy time fell by 106.5 ms. With the kernel factor of that server (2.95 to 3.05, est.), this model gives 1.90 to 1.93 times for our cell with 8 users and prompt 1,024 (est.). A factor on the whole busy time gives 2.95 to 3.05 times.
Decode: the factor divides the whole busy time. The decode factor is a ratio of whole busy times of attention worker 0 [Ref19]. So the join, the join wait and the pages of the pass in progress are already in it. With 8 users the mean busy time per decode step fell 1.18 to 1.19 times in three A/B runs on delphi-3bda [Ref23]. If the join wait of a decode step did not shrink with the kernel, the decode range would be -4.5 % to +6.5 % (est.).
Sensitivity of the prefill model. If the factor divided the whole busy time, Part B would give a TTFT fall of 5 to 24 % (est.), range 4 to 28 %. Parts A and B together would give 34 to 42 % (est.), range 22 to 48 %.

answers.open_points:
1. Choice of the working model. I recommend a fourth variant, (d), which the task did not list: the prefill factor divides only the part of the busy time that grows with the full-page K tokens. Reasons: it is the same split as the fit that produced the factor, it needs no assumption about the join wait, the fold work or the cost of a partial-page K token, and it is the only variant that reproduces the measured whole-timer ratio on delphi-3bda (1.90-1.93 against 1.88). Of the three listed variants (c) is the best, but it is 12 to 14 % too high against that measurement at prompt 1,024, because T2 minus T5 also contains the fold work of the join. If the author prefers (c), the numbers are in the table above: Part B 4 to 23 %, range 3 to 26 %, Parts A and B 33 to 42 %, range 20 to 47 %. All proposed text is written for (d).
2. Decode keeps the whole-timer model on purpose. Its factor is a ratio of whole busy times (Ref19), and the 8-user A/B runs give the same 1.18 to 1.19 on the mean busy time. The proposed text adds the range for a fixed join wait (-4.5 % to +6.5 %) as a sensitivity.
3. Not tested: gen_design.py was not run, so the proposed generator text and the two new table columns are untested. Only the predict.py change was run, in a scratch copy.
4. Limits of the delphi-3bda check: one run per arm, other models (128-wide heads, 36 or 32 attention layers), 20 workers instead of 40, another server. The shares used in the check are those of Qwen3.5 4B. It is a plausibility check, and the proposed bullet says 'one run per arm'. No A/B with the statistics exists for 1 user, so the 51 % full-page share of the 1-user, prompt-1,024 cell has no such check. Insufficient data.
5. Wait for K and V. No timer isolates it. Hint from the data: the attention wait changes by at most 0.23 ms (1 user) and 0.46 ms (8 users) per pass between the prompt lengths while the full-page scoring gets 9 times longer, so today's wait for K and V is small (est.) and most of the attention wait is the wait for Q (est.). After Part B the full-page scoring at prompt 1,024 would take about 0.17 ms per layer with 1 user (est.). Whether K and V are ready by then is not known. In the qwen-3-4b A/B (8 users) the pass wall followed the busy time (99.7 of 106.5 ms). The proposed open-point bullet covers this.
6. Not modeled, for the author to decide: under Part B the attention workers' remaining AVX-512 work (pages of the pass, fold: 1.5 ms per pass with 1 user and 6.4 ms with 8 users, est.) may run at the AMX clock. At 2.40 GHz that adds 0.2 ms (1 user) or 0.8 ms (8 users) per pass, at 1.90 GHz 0.6 ms or 2.7 ms (est.). In TTFT terms at most 0.5 to 1.3 percentage points (est.). The page models such a clock cost for Part A only. The delphi-3bda A/B already contains the effect at that server's 92 % clock.

1. Decision for the author: Part A alone cannot be run in a build that holds Part B. The two switches of section 5.6 give Part 0 with AVX-512, Part 0 with Part B, and Parts A and B. So the proposal keeps Part B equal in both runs of task 6 and checks the Part A range with a sum of two measured falls. The alternative is a second new switch that turns the 256-wide attention kernel off alone, or a task 6 build without Part B. Then the total is one comparison: base run against a Part A run with AVX-512 attention, and the reviewer's example (2.235 s to 2.060 s) is the A/B run itself. I did not propose the switch because it adds a feature to the design.

2. The Part B rule and the Part A sum rule rest on one assumption of the model: the seconds that one part saves do not depend on the other part. Insufficient data. A run of Part B on the base build (a branch without Part 0) would test it for Part B. A Part A run with AVX-512 attention would test it for Part A.

answers.open_points:
1. Author decision, third piece. The checks keep the third piece as an FP32 number and only test whether it is a bf16 value. The proposed text says that the plane keeps its upper 16 bits (truncation). That is what r3_split_facts.py computes as 'largest part that 3 bf16 values do not hold'. Confirm that the kernel will do this.
2. Author decision, small values. The proposed Fallback text says that values below 2^-103 take no fallback and that their loss is part of the error band. The page implies this today and does not state it. If the author wants a fallback for small values instead, the last two sentences of that change must be replaced.
3. Mixed rules in the numeric bullets of section 5.4. The ranges '0.005 to 0.10 %', 'up to 67 increments', '0.3 to 1.1 times' and '0.3 to 3.2 times' come from three checks, of which two (prototype, skeptic) round the pieces to nearest. For truncation alone, vm_checks.out gives 0.0061 to 0.1015 % of the output words. I did not recompute the other ranges per rule. The new bullet 'Which rule the numeric checks used' discloses the mix. A re-run of the prototype with the truncation rule would remove it.
4. Insufficient data: how TDPBF16PS treats subnormal inputs and results was not measured and the Intel manual was not re-read here (no network). A unit test in task 3 on delphi-3b35 resolves it: one tile product with a subnormal bf16 input and one with a subnormal result.
5. Insufficient data: how often state values of the real model are below 2^-103. The block-form scenarios use start states of size 0.01 to 1e3, and 5e37 in case F3. verify-math/vm_subnormal.out counts 0 subnormal state values in 3 synthetic scenarios. A histogram of the state sizes from a real Qwen3.5 4B run would resolve it.
6. Not covered by any check: the block form with state values at the top of the range above 5e37, and the block form with state values below 2^-103. Only the split itself was checked exhaustively at both ends.
7. Side effect for task 3 (no page change proposed): for values below 2^-103 the two FP32 subtractions of the split produce subnormal results in AVX-512 code. tron sets no flush-to-zero mode, so the CPU takes its slow path there. The risk bullet of section 6 about subnormal numbers already covers the measurement.

answers.verdict: The reviewer is right. The interval "0.2 to 0.4 us" fits only the two runs of stage 1 (an AVX-512 split of 0.21 to 0.26 us and a tile run of 0.45 us at 2.40 GHz, est.). The block kernel also has one AVX-512 run of 2.4 to 3.0 us (stage 3 plus the split of Delta) and 16 runs of only 64 FMAs (13 to 16 ns), and the page compares these single runs with full turns of the clock probe. Words used here: a run is a stretch of tile work alone or of AVX-512 work alone, and a turn is one tile run plus the AVX-512 run next to it.
